decks.title: Triangles — Part 1: Similar figures and the Basic Proportionality Theorem
goals: Distinguish similar and congruent figures using equal angles and proportional sides
State and prove the Basic Proportionality Theorem
Find unknown lengths in a triangle using the theorem
Prove two lines parallel using the converse of the theorem

slides.heading: Triangles, Part 1: Similar figures and the Basic Proportionality Theorem
slides.body_md: Same shape, different size — and the theorem that turns a parallel line into a ratio.

visual.alt: Two triangles of exactly the same shape: triangle PQR is triangle ABC enlarged 1.75 times, so every side of PQR is 1.75 times the matching side of ABC and the angles are unchanged.
visual.caption: Same shape, different size: △PQR is an enlargement of △ABC (scale factor 1.75).

slides.narration: Welcome to Triangles, part one. Look at the two triangles on the screen. One is bigger, but they have exactly the same shape. In this lesson we pin down what "same shape" means in mathematics, and then we prove a powerful result called the Basic Proportionality Theorem. By the end, you will find unknown lengths inside a triangle using nothing more than a parallel line and a ratio.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Tell **similar** figures from **congruent** ones, with examples and counter-examples
State and **prove** the Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT)
Use BPT to find unknown lengths in a triangle
Use the **converse** of BPT to prove that two lines are parallel
slides.narration: Here are your four goals for this part. Notice the word prove in the second goal. The proof of this theorem is in your syllabus, and board papers ask for it as a five-mark question. So we will build the proof slowly, one step per slide, and you will see exactly where each mark comes from.

slides.heading: Congruent or similar?
columns: **Congruent** ($\cong$): same shape **and** same size. One figure fits exactly on the other.
**Similar** ($\sim$): same shape, size may differ. One figure is an enlargement or reduction of the other.

visual.alt: Comparison table: congruent figures have the same shape and size with equal angles and equal sides; similar figures have the same shape, equal angles and sides in one common ratio, but the size may differ.
visual.caption: Every congruent pair is similar (ratio 1), but not every similar pair is congruent.

slides.narration: Think of two ten-rupee coins. They match perfectly, so they are congruent. Now think of your passport photo and the same photo printed as a poster. The poster is much bigger, but faces are not stretched or squashed. That is similarity. Every congruent pair is also similar, with a ratio of one, but most similar pairs are not congruent.

slides.heading: Similar polygons need both conditions
slides.body_md: Two polygons with the same number of sides are **similar** when (1) all corresponding angles are equal **and** (2) all corresponding sides are in the same ratio.

visual.alt: Left: square ABCD with side 2 cm. Middle: rectangle EFGH, 3.5 cm by 2 cm, with right angles like the square but sides not in one ratio. Right: rhombus IJKM with side 2 cm, sides in ratio 1 to 1 with the square but with a 60 degree angle instead of 90 degrees.
visual.caption: Square vs rectangle: angles equal, sides not proportional. Square vs rhombus: sides proportional, angles not equal. Neither pair is similar.

slides.narration: Why insist on both conditions? Look at the square and the rectangle. All their angles are ninety degrees, yet the rectangle is stretched, so they are not similar. Now compare the square with the rhombus. Every side ratio is one to one, but the rhombus is tilted, so its angles differ. Equal angles alone, or proportional sides alone, are not enough for polygons in general.

slides.heading: The order of letters and the scale factor
slides.body_md: Writing $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ matches the vertices in order: $A \leftrightarrow P$, $B \leftrightarrow Q$, $C \leftrightarrow R$.
bullets: $k$ is the **scale factor**; $k = 1$ means the triangles are congruent.
math: \angle A = \angle P,\quad \angle B = \angle Q,\quad \angle C = \angle R
slides.narration: A similarity statement is like a seating plan. The first letter sits with the first letter, the second with the second, and the third with the third. So if triangle A B C is similar to triangle P Q R, side A B goes with side P Q, never with Q R. Most mistakes in this chapter come from mixing up this order, so always read the statement letter by letter.

slides.heading: Quick check: which figures are always similar?
slides.body_md: Answer before you move on.
slides.narration: Your turn. Keep both conditions in mind: equal angles and proportional sides. Which kind of figure passes both tests whatever its size? Try to find a counter-example for each wrong option before you choose.

slides.heading: The set-up: a line parallel to one side
slides.body_md: In $\triangle ABC$, a line parallel to $BC$ cuts $AB$ at $D$ and $AC$ at $E$, at two distinct points.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with D on side AB and E on side AC. The segment DE is parallel to the base BC; D divides AB, and E divides AC, in the same ratio 2 to 3.
visual.caption: DE ∥ BC. Here AD : DB = AE : EC = 2 : 3.

slides.narration: Now for the big idea. Take any triangle and draw a line parallel to one side, cutting the other two sides. Imagine a ladder leaning against a wall, with a rung parallel to the ground. The rung cuts both rails in the same proportion. In this picture, D cuts side A B and E cuts side A C, and both cuts are two parts to three.

slides.heading: Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales)
slides.body_md: If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to meet the other two sides at distinct points, it divides those two sides in the same ratio.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with D on side AB and E on side AC. The segment DE is parallel to the base BC; D divides AB, and E divides AC, in the same ratio 2 to 3.
visual.caption: DE ∥ BC. Here AD : DB = AE : EC = 2 : 3.

slides.narration: Here is the theorem in words. A line parallel to one side divides the other two sides in the same ratio. It is also called Thales' theorem, after the Greek mathematician who is said to have measured the height of a pyramid from its shadow. Learn the statement exactly. In a proof question, writing the statement correctly is usually the first mark you earn.

slides.heading: Proof, step 0: given, to prove, construction
bullets: **Given:** in $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$, with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$.
**To prove:** $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$.
**Construction:** join $BE$ and $CD$; draw $EM \perp AB$ and $DN \perp AC$.

visual.alt: The construction for the proof: in triangle ABC with DE parallel to BC, the segments BE and CD are joined, EM is drawn perpendicular to AB with M on AB, and DN is drawn perpendicular to AC with N on AC.
visual.caption: Construction: join BE and CD; draw EM ⊥ AB and DN ⊥ AC.

slides.narration: Every proof starts with three lines: what is given, what we must prove, and any construction. The construction here looks strange at first. We join B to E and C to D, and we drop two perpendiculars. Why? Because the proof works with areas of triangles, and the perpendiculars give us their heights. Copy the figure neatly. The board awards a mark for a correct figure.

slides.heading: Proof, step 1: triangles ADE and BDE share a height
slides.body_md: Area of a triangle $= \tfrac12 \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$. Take $AD$ and $DB$ as bases; $EM$ is the height of both.

visual.alt: Triangles ADE and BDE are shaded. Their bases AD and DB lie on the same line AB, and the perpendicular EM from E to AB is the height of both triangles.
visual.caption: △ADE and △BDE: bases AD and DB on line AB, common height EM.

math: \frac{\operatorname{ar}(\triangle ADE)}{\operatorname{ar}(\triangle BDE)} = \frac{\tfrac12 \cdot AD \cdot EM}{\tfrac12 \cdot DB \cdot EM} = \frac{AD}{DB} \qquad (1)
slides.narration: Look at the two shaded triangles, A D E and B D E. Their bases, A D and D B, lie on the same line, and they share the same top corner E. So they have the same height, E M. When we divide one area by the other, the half and the height cancel. What remains is A D over D B. Call this result one.

slides.heading: Proof, step 2: triangles ADE and DEC share a height
slides.body_md: Now take $AE$ and $EC$ as bases; $DN$ is the height of both triangles.

visual.alt: Triangles ADE and DEC are shaded. Their bases AE and EC lie on the same line AC, and the perpendicular DN from D to AC is the height of both triangles.
visual.caption: △ADE and △DEC: bases AE and EC on line AC, common height DN.

math: \frac{\operatorname{ar}(\triangle ADE)}{\operatorname{ar}(\triangle DEC)} = \frac{\tfrac12 \cdot AE \cdot DN}{\tfrac12 \cdot EC \cdot DN} = \frac{AE}{EC} \qquad (2)
slides.narration: Same trick on the other side. Triangles A D E and D E C have bases A E and E C on the line A C, and both reach up to the corner D. Their common height is D N. Dividing the areas, everything cancels except A E over E C. Call this result two. Notice that triangle A D E appears in both results. That is the bridge we need.

slides.heading: Proof, step 3: the key pair of equal areas
slides.body_md: $\triangle BDE$ and $\triangle DEC$ stand on the **same base** $DE$ and lie **between the same parallels** $DE$ and $BC$.

visual.alt: Triangles BDE and CED are shaded. Both stand on the same base DE, and their third vertices B and C lie on the line BC, which is parallel to DE, so both triangles have the same height.
visual.caption: Same base DE, between the same parallels DE and BC ⇒ equal areas.

slides.narration: This is the only place where the parallel line is used, so it is the heart of the proof. Both shaded triangles sit on the base D E. Their top corners, B and C, lie on the line B C, which is parallel to D E. So both triangles have the same height and therefore the same area. In the exam, you must write this reason in full to get the mark.

slides.heading: Proof, step 4: put it together
bullets: Hence $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$, which was to be proved.
Other forms: flip and add 1 to get $\dfrac{AB}{AD} = \dfrac{AC}{AE}$, so $\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{AE}{AC}$ and $\dfrac{DB}{AB} = \dfrac{EC}{AC}$.
slides.narration: Now chain the three results. Start from A D over D B, swap in the area ratio from result one, replace the bottom area using result three, and finish with result two. That gives A E over E C. Done! Also learn the other forms on the slide. A D over A B equals A E over A C is often the quickest way to find a missing length.

slides.heading: Quick check: which ratio does BPT NOT give?
slides.body_md: One of these looks right but is a classic trap.
slides.narration: Think carefully here. The theorem talks about the two sides that are cut. It says nothing directly about the parallel segment itself. Which option sneaks that segment into a ratio in the wrong way?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a missing length
slides.body_md: In $\triangle PQR$, $ST \parallel QR$ with $S$ on $PQ$ and $T$ on $PR$. $PS = 2.4$ cm, $SQ = 3.6$ cm, $PR = 7.5$ cm. Find $PT$ and $TR$.
bullets: **Step 2 —** By BPT, $\dfrac{PS}{PQ} = \dfrac{PT}{PR}$, so $\dfrac{2.4}{6} = \dfrac{PT}{7.5}$.
**Check —** $\dfrac{PS}{SQ} = \dfrac{2.4}{3.6} = \dfrac23$ and $\dfrac{PT}{TR} = \dfrac{3}{4.5} = \dfrac23$. ✓

visual.alt: Triangle PQR drawn to scale with S on PQ and T on PR, ST parallel to QR. PS is 2.4 centimetres, SQ is 3.6 centimetres and the whole side PR is 7.5 centimetres; PT is unknown.
visual.caption: ST ∥ QR, PR = 7.5 cm. Find PT and TR.

slides.narration: When the question gives a whole side, like P R here, use the form with whole sides: a part over the whole on one side equals the part over the whole on the other side. That avoids messy algebra. Then always check your answer with the original form of the theorem. Both ratios come out as two thirds, so we can be confident.

slides.heading: The converse: proving lines parallel
slides.body_md: If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.
bullets: Statement only: the proof of the converse is not asked in the 2026–27 syllabus.
Use it when a question says **prove** or **check** that two lines are parallel.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with D on AB and E on AC. AD is 3 and DB is 4, AE is 3.3 and EC is 4.4, so both sides are cut in the ratio 3 to 4 and the dashed segment DE comes out parallel to BC.
visual.caption: Equal ratios (3 : 4 = 3.3 : 4.4) force DE ∥ BC.

slides.narration: The theorem also works backwards. If you can show that the two ratios are equal, the line must be parallel. This converse is your tool whenever a question asks you to prove two lines parallel using lengths. You only need its statement, not its proof. In the figure, three to four equals three point three to four point four, so D E is parallel to B C.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: is MN parallel to YZ?
slides.body_md: In $\triangle XYZ$, $M$ is on $XY$ and $N$ is on $XZ$. $XM = 3$ cm, $MY = 5$ cm, $XN = 4.5$ cm, $NZ = 7.5$ cm. Is $MN \parallel YZ$?
bullets: **Step 1 —** $\dfrac{XM}{MY} = \dfrac{3}{5} = 0.6$.
**Step 3 —** The ratios are equal, so by the converse of BPT, $MN \parallel YZ$.
**Contrast —** if $NZ$ were $7$ cm, $\dfrac{4.5}{7} \approx 0.64 \neq 0.6$, so $MN$ would **not** be parallel.

visual.alt: Triangle XYZ with M on XY and N on XZ. XM is 3 centimetres, MY is 5, XN is 4.5 and NZ is 7.5; the dashed segment MN is to be tested for being parallel to YZ.
visual.caption: Is MN ∥ YZ? Compare XM : MY with XN : NZ.

slides.narration: Compute each ratio separately and simplify. Here both are zero point six, so the converse lets us conclude that the lines are parallel. Always name the reason, converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem, in your answer. And notice the contrast. If the ratios differ even slightly, the line is not parallel, because a parallel line would be forced to cut the sides in equal ratios.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: three parallel roads (part 1)
slides.body_md: Three straight roads in a Pune housing colony are parallel. Lane 1 crosses them at $A, B, C$; lane 2 at $P, Q, R$. Prove that $\dfrac{AB}{BC} = \dfrac{PQ}{QR}$.
bullets: **Construction —** join $AR$; let it meet the middle road at $X$.
**Step 1 —** In $\triangle ACR$, $BX \parallel CR$ (parts of parallel roads), so by BPT $\dfrac{AB}{BC} = \dfrac{AX}{XR}$.

visual.alt: Three horizontal parallel roads. Lane 1 crosses them at A, B and C; lane 2 crosses them at P, Q and R. The construction line AR, dashed, meets the middle road at X.
visual.caption: Roads AP ∥ BQ ∥ CR. Construction: join AR, meeting the middle road at X.

slides.narration: The theorem works only inside a triangle, but here we have two lanes and three roads, with no triangle in sight. The trick is to create one. Join A to R. Now look at the triangle A C R. The middle road cuts it, and that road is parallel to the bottom road. So the Basic Proportionality Theorem gives our first ratio.

slides.heading: Worked example 3 (part 2): finish, then use it
bullets: **Step 2 —** In $\triangle RAP$, $XQ \parallel AP$, so by BPT $\dfrac{RX}{XA} = \dfrac{RQ}{QP}$, i.e. $\dfrac{AX}{XR} = \dfrac{PQ}{QR}$.
**Step 3 —** From steps 1 and 2, $\dfrac{AB}{BC} = \dfrac{PQ}{QR}$. $\blacksquare$

visual.alt: The same three parallel roads drawn to scale. On lane 1, AB is 120 metres and BC is 180 metres. On lane 2, PQ is 150 metres and QR is unknown. The dashed line AR passes through X on the middle road.
visual.caption: Drawn to scale: AB = 120 m, BC = 180 m, PQ = 150 m. Find QR.

slides.narration: Now use the same line A R in the other triangle, R A P. This time the middle road is parallel to the top road. The theorem gives a second ratio, and both ratios share A X over X R, so they are equal. That proves the result. A town planner can use it to find a length without walking it: two hundred and twenty-five metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: a length from BPT
slides.body_md: Use the form of the theorem that matches the lengths you are given.
slides.narration: Write the ratio of the two parts on one side and set it equal to the ratio of the two parts on the other side. Then cross-multiply carefully.

slides.heading: Quick check: assertion and reason
slides.body_md: Decide whether each statement is true, then whether the reason explains the assertion.
slides.narration: First test the assertion with numbers. Then ask yourself which theorem actually lets you conclude that two lines are parallel. Is it the theorem, or its converse?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Similar figures: equal corresponding angles **and** proportional corresponding sides.
Order matters: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ pairs $A$–$P$, $B$–$Q$, $C$–$R$.
BPT: $DE \parallel BC \Rightarrow \dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$ (proof by areas).
Converse: $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC} \Rightarrow DE \parallel BC$.
Three parallel lines cut any two transversals in the same ratio.

rows: Three parallel lines cut two lines
The intercepts are in the same ratio

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the Basic Proportionality Theorem and its other forms give equal ratios from a parallel line; the converse gives a parallel line from equal ratios; three parallel lines cut any two transversals in the same ratio.

slides.narration: Let us recap. Similar figures have equal angles and proportional sides, and the order of letters tells you which parts match. A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides in the same ratio, and we proved it using areas. Its converse proves lines parallel. In part two, you will learn quick tests for similar triangles and use them to measure tall buildings.

slides.heading: Exam tips: earning every mark
bullets: BPT proof (5 marks): statement with given and to prove 1, figure with construction 1, each area ratio 1 + 1, equal areas with reason and conclusion 1.
In step 3, write the full reason: "same base $DE$ and between the same parallels $DE$ and $BC$".
Trap: $\dfrac{AD}{DB} \neq \dfrac{DE}{BC}$. The parallel segment compares with the **whole** side: $\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{AD}{AB}$ (Part 2).
Proving lines parallel? Show both ratios separately, then name "converse of BPT".
Keep units, and check your answer by substituting back into the ratio.
slides.narration: Here is how examiners award marks. In the theorem proof, the figure, the given and to-prove lines, each area ratio and the final conclusion all carry marks, so never skip a line. The most common error is comparing the parallel segment with a part of a side instead of the whole side. And when you prove lines parallel, always write the name of the converse as your reason.

decks.title: Triangles — Part 2: Criteria for similarity and applications
goals: State the AA, SSS and SAS similarity criteria and match vertices correctly
Choose the right criterion for a given figure
Prove two triangles similar with a reason for every step
Find unknown sides and solve height-and-shadow problems using similarity

slides.heading: Triangles, Part 2: Criteria for similarity and real-world heights
slides.body_md: Three quick tests for similar triangles — and how a shadow can measure a monument.

visual.alt: A short vertical pole AB and a tall vertical tower PQ stand on level ground. Parallel sun rays AC and PR make the same angle theta with the ground, so the triangles ABC and PQR have a right angle and an equal angle theta.
visual.caption: Vertical objects + parallel sun rays ⇒ equal angles ⇒ similar triangles (AA).

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Look at the pole and the tower on the screen. At the same moment, the sun's rays hit both at the same angle. That simple fact lets you find the height of a tower, a temple or a monument with just a measuring tape. First we learn three quick tests for similar triangles. Then we put them to work.

slides.heading: Recap: what similar triangles look like
slides.body_md: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ means equal corresponding angles **and** corresponding sides in one ratio.

visual.alt: Triangles ABC and PQR with angles 70, 60 and 50 degrees at A, B, C and at P, Q, R. Every side of PQR is 1.5 times the matching side of ABC.
visual.caption: △ABC ∼ △PQR: equal angles, sides in the ratio 1 : 1.5.

slides.narration: Here are two similar triangles. The angles match, seventy, sixty and fifty degrees, and every side of the bigger triangle is one and a half times the matching side of the smaller one. To prove similarity from the definition, we would need to check three angles and three ratios. That is six checks. Can we get away with fewer?

slides.heading: Shortcut tests: the similarity criteria
slides.body_md: For triangles, a few well-chosen facts force all six to be true. These are the **criteria for similarity**.
bullets: **AA** (angle–angle)
**SSS** (side–side–side)
**SAS** (side–angle–side)
Statements only: their proofs are not asked in the 2026–27 syllabus.
slides.narration: Triangles are special. Unlike other polygons, a triangle is rigid. Once a few parts are fixed, its shape is fixed. That is why we have shortcut tests. There are three of them: angle angle, side side side, and side angle side. You need to state them correctly and use them in proofs. You do not need to prove them.

slides.heading: AA criterion
slides.body_md: If two angles of one triangle are equal to two angles of another, the triangles are similar.

visual.alt: Triangles ABC and DEF of different sizes. Angle A and angle D are both 65 degrees; angle B and angle E are both 45 degrees. The third angles C and F must both be 70 degrees.
visual.caption: ∠A = ∠D and ∠B = ∠E ⇒ △ABC ∼ △DEF (AA).

math: \angle A = \angle D,\ \angle B = \angle E \;\Longrightarrow\; \triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF
slides.narration: If two pairs of angles match, the third pair must match too, because the angles of every triangle add up to one hundred and eighty degrees. In the figure, sixty-five and forty-five force the third angle to be seventy in both triangles. Some books call this the A A A criterion. A A is simply the shorter way to use it.

slides.heading: SSS criterion
slides.body_md: If all three sides of one triangle are in the same ratio to the three sides of another, the triangles are similar.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with sides AB 4, BC 6 and CA 5 centimetres, and triangle PQR with sides PQ 6, QR 9 and RP 7.5 centimetres, drawn to the same scale. Each side of PQR is 1.5 times the matching side of ABC.
visual.caption: 6/4 = 9/6 = 7.5/5 = 1.5 ⇒ △ABC ∼ △PQR (SSS). Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: With side side side, you pair the sides by size. Shortest with shortest, middle with middle, longest with longest. Then divide. If all three ratios are equal, here one point five, the triangles are similar, and equal angles sit opposite matching sides. If even one ratio is different, the triangles are not similar.

slides.heading: SAS criterion
slides.body_md: If one angle of a triangle equals one angle of another, and the sides **including** these angles are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with AB 3 and AC 4 centimetres and a 50 degree angle at A between them; triangle DEF with DE 4.5 and DF 6 centimetres and a 50 degree angle at D between them.
visual.caption: DE/AB = DF/AC = 1.5 and the included angles are equal ⇒ △ABC ∼ △DEF (SAS).

slides.narration: Side angle side needs two sides and the angle between them. The word including is important. The equal angle must be the one formed by the two sides you compared. Here, A B and A C meet at angle A, and D E and D F meet at angle D. Both angles are fifty degrees and both ratios are one point five, so the triangles are similar.

slides.heading: Trap: SSA is not a criterion
slides.body_md: Two sides and a **non-included** angle can fit two different triangles, so they prove nothing.

visual.alt: Side AB is 7 centimetres and angle A is 40 degrees. A circle of radius 5 centimetres around B cuts the ray from A at two points, C1 and C2, so two different triangles ABC1 and ABC2 both have AB 7, BC 5 and angle A 40 degrees.
visual.caption: Two sides and a non-included angle can give two different triangles, so SSA proves nothing.

slides.narration: Here is why the angle must be included. Side A B is seven, angle A is forty degrees, and side B C must be five. Swing a five centimetre compass around B. It hits the base line twice, at C one and C two. Both triangles match the data, but they have different shapes. So two sides and an angle that is not between them is not a valid test.

slides.heading: The three criteria side by side

headers: Where the facts usually come from
rows: Two pairs of corresponding angles equal
Parallel lines (corresponding or alternate angles), a common angle, vertically opposite angles, right angles
The third pair is then equal automatically
All three pairs of corresponding sides in one ratio
Pair shortest with shortest and longest with longest
Two pairs of sides in one ratio and the angle between them equal
A common or vertically opposite angle between the known sides
The equal angle must be the included angle

visual.alt: Table comparing the three similarity criteria: AA needs two pairs of equal angles, SSS needs all three side ratios equal, SAS needs two side ratios equal and the included angles equal, with typical sources of the facts and the common trap for each.

slides.narration: Here is the whole toolbox in one table. Read the third column carefully. In most problems the facts are hidden in the figure: a pair of parallel lines gives equal alternate angles, two lines crossing give vertically opposite angles, and two triangles that share a corner share an angle. Spotting these hidden facts is the real skill in this chapter.

slides.heading: Which criterion should I use?

nodes.label: Two triangles: what do you know?
Two pairs of corresponding angles equal?
Two side ratios equal and the angle between them equal?
Not proved yet: look for parallel lines, a common angle or vertically opposite angles

visual.alt: Decision chart: first ask whether two pairs of angles are equal, which gives AA; if not, whether all three side ratios are equal, which gives SSS; if not, whether two side ratios and the included angle are equal, which gives SAS; otherwise look for hidden facts such as parallel lines or common angles and start again.

slides.narration: When you face a new figure, run through this chart. First look for two pairs of equal angles, because A A is the most common route. If you only have lengths, try side side side. If you have two lengths and an angle, make sure the angle is the one between them. If nothing works, go back to the figure and hunt for parallel lines or shared angles.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the criterion
slides.body_md: Which criterion do these facts satisfy?
slides.narration: Look at where the equal angle sits. Is it between the two sides that are in proportion? And check that the letters of the two triangles are matched in the right order.

slides.heading: Read the correspondence from the statement
slides.body_md: If $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle QRP$, the letters pair up by position, not alphabetically.

rows: A ↔ Q, B ↔ R, C ↔ P

visual.alt: Table reading the statement triangle ABC similar to triangle QRP: A matches Q, B matches R, C matches P, so angle A equals angle Q and so on, and AB over QR equals BC over RP equals CA over PQ.
visual.caption: Read the letters position by position: 1st with 1st, 2nd with 2nd, 3rd with 3rd.

slides.narration: Suppose you are told that triangle A B C is similar to triangle Q R P. Do not pair A with P just because they come first in the alphabet. Read the statement position by position. First letters, A and Q. Second, B and R. Third, C and P. Then write the side ratios from those pairs. This habit alone saves many marks.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: unknown sides from AA
slides.body_md: In $\triangle PQR$ and $\triangle STU$, $\angle P = \angle S$ and $\angle Q = \angle T$. $PQ = 6$ cm, $QR = 7.5$ cm, $ST = 8$ cm, $SU = 12$ cm. Find $TU$ and $PR$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Two pairs of angles are equal, so $\triangle PQR \sim \triangle STU$ (AA), with $P \leftrightarrow S$, $Q \leftrightarrow T$, $R \leftrightarrow U$.
**Step 2 —** $\dfrac{ST}{PQ} = \dfrac{TU}{QR} = \dfrac{SU}{PR}$, and $\dfrac{ST}{PQ} = \dfrac{8}{6} = \dfrac43$.
**Step 3 —** $TU = \dfrac43 \times 7.5 = 10$ cm; $PR = \dfrac{12}{4/3} = 9$ cm.

visual.alt: Triangles PQR and STU with angle P equal to angle S (marked alpha) and angle Q equal to angle T (marked beta). PQ is 6, QR is 7.5, ST is 8 and SU is 12 centimetres; PR and TU are unknown.
visual.caption: ∠P = ∠S, ∠Q = ∠T. Lengths in cm; find TU and PR.

slides.narration: First name the criterion and write the similarity in the correct order. Then find the scale factor from the one pair of sides you know completely, here eight over six, which is four thirds. Going from the small triangle to the big one, multiply by four thirds. Going back, divide. Finish by checking that all three ratios agree.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a median cut by a parallel line (part 1)
slides.body_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $AD$ is a median. A line parallel to $BC$ meets $AB$, $AD$, $AC$ at $P$, $R$, $Q$. Prove that $PR = RQ$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** In $\triangle APR$ and $\triangle ABD$: $\angle A$ is common and $\angle APR = \angle ABD$ (corresponding angles, $PR \parallel BD$).
So $\triangle APR \sim \triangle ABD$ (AA), giving $\dfrac{PR}{BD} = \dfrac{AR}{AD}$.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with median AD, so D is the midpoint of BC. A segment PQ parallel to BC meets AB at P, AD at R and AC at Q. Triangle APR is shaded inside the larger triangle ABD.
visual.caption: AD is a median (BD = DC) and PQ ∥ BC. Prove PR = RQ.

slides.narration: Here is a proof where we need similarity, not just the proportionality theorem, because we want a ratio involving the parallel segment itself. Look at the small shaded triangle A P R inside the bigger triangle A B D. They share the angle at A, and the parallel line gives equal corresponding angles at P and B. That is A A, and it gives our first ratio.

slides.heading: Worked example 2 (part 2): finish the proof
bullets: **Step 2 —** Similarly $\triangle ARQ \sim \triangle ADC$ (AA: common $\angle A$, $\angle ARQ = \angle ADC$), so $\dfrac{RQ}{DC} = \dfrac{AR}{AD}$.
**Step 3 —** Hence $\dfrac{PR}{BD} = \dfrac{RQ}{DC}$.
**Step 4 —** $BD = DC$ ($D$ is the midpoint), so $PR = RQ$. $\blacksquare$
slides.narration: Repeat the idea on the right-hand side to get a second ratio. Both ratios equal A R over A D, so they equal each other. Finally, use the one fact we have not touched yet: a median goes to the midpoint, so B D equals D C. The denominators are equal, so the numerators are equal too. Notice how each step uses exactly one given fact.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the triangles
slides.body_md: Find the third angles first, then pair equal angles.
slides.narration: Work out the missing angle in each triangle. Then match equal angles and write the vertices in that order. Watch out: the option that looks most natural may pair the wrong letters.

slides.heading: Why shadows give similar triangles
bullets: Objects stand **vertical**: right angles at the ground.
Sun rays are **parallel**: at one moment they make the same angle with level ground.
Two equal angles ⇒ similar triangles (AA), so height : shadow is the same for every object.

visual.alt: A short vertical pole AB and a tall vertical tower PQ stand on level ground. Parallel sun rays AC and PR make the same angle theta with the ground, so the triangles ABC and PQR have a right angle and an equal angle theta.
visual.caption: Vertical objects + parallel sun rays ⇒ equal angles ⇒ similar triangles (AA).

math: \frac{\text{height of object}}{\text{its shadow}} = \frac{\text{height of stick}}{\text{its shadow}}
slides.narration: The sun is so far away that its rays arrive parallel. So at any one moment, every vertical object on level ground makes a triangle with its shadow, and all these triangles have the same angles. That means the ratio of height to shadow is the same for a stick, a person or a monument. This only works at the same time and on level ground.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the height of the Qutub Minar
slides.body_md: In Delhi, a student $1.6$ m tall casts a $2.4$ m shadow. At the same moment, the Qutub Minar casts a shadow of $108.75$ m. Find its height $h$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Right angles at the ground and the same sun angle, so $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ (AA).
**Step 2 —** $\dfrac{PQ}{AB} = \dfrac{QR}{BC}$, so $\dfrac{h}{1.6} = \dfrac{108.75}{2.4}$.
**Sense check —** height : shadow $= 1.6 : 2.4 = 2 : 3$ for both. ✓

visual.alt: Left: a student AB, 1.6 metres tall, with a shadow BC of 2.4 metres. Right: the Qutub Minar PQ of unknown height h with a shadow QR of 108.75 metres. Both triangles have a right angle at the base and the same sun angle theta.
visual.caption: The two triangles have the same shape but are drawn at different scales. △ABC ∼ △PQR (AA).

slides.narration: The Qutub Minar is about seventy-two and a half metres tall, but you cannot exactly drop a tape from the top! With similar triangles, a student and a tape on the ground are enough. Set up the ratio with heights on top and shadows at the bottom on both sides. Then a quick sense check: both objects have height to shadow of two to three.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a lamp post on a Pune street
slides.body_md: A lamp is fixed $6$ m above the ground on a post. A boy $1.5$ m tall stands $4.5$ m from the foot of the post. How long is his shadow? How far away must he stand for a $2$ m shadow?
bullets: **Step 1 —** $\triangle SBH \sim \triangle SOL$ (AA: right angles at $B$ and $O$; $\angle S$ common).
**Step 2 —** $\dfrac{BH}{OL} = \dfrac{SB}{SO}$: $\dfrac{1.5}{6} = \dfrac{x}{x + 4.5}$, so $6x = 1.5x + 6.75$ and $x = 1.5$ m.
**Step 3 —** For a $2$ m shadow: $\dfrac{1.5}{6} = \dfrac{2}{2 + d}$, so $2 + d = 8$ and $d = 6$ m.

visual.alt: Drawn to scale: a lamp at L on top of a 6 metre post LO. A boy BH, 1.5 metres tall, stands 4.5 metres from the foot O. The light ray from L just grazes his head H and reaches the ground at S, the tip of his shadow BS of unknown length x.
visual.caption: △SBH ∼ △SOL (AA: right angles and the common angle at S).

slides.narration: A lamp post is different from the sun. Its light spreads out from one point, so the triangles share the angle at the tip of the shadow instead of having parallel rays. The big triangle uses the whole distance from the post to the shadow tip, that is x plus four point five. Forgetting to add the distance is the most common mistake here.

slides.heading: Quick check: a tower from a stick
slides.body_md: Same time, level ground.
slides.narration: Set up height over shadow for the stick and for the tower, and make them equal. Keep heights on top on both sides.

slides.heading: Writing a similarity proof for full marks
bullets: Write the pair of triangles **in matching order**: "In $\triangle APR$ and $\triangle ABD$".
One fact per line, each with its reason in brackets: (common), (corresponding angles, $PR \parallel BD$), (vertically opposite angles).
Name the criterion: "$\therefore \triangle APR \sim \triangle ABD$ (AA)".
Then write the ratio you need and finish with the required result.

visual.caption: Board marking awards marks for the figure and for each justified step, not only for the last line.

slides.narration: Examiners mark proofs line by line. Write the two triangles in matching order, give each fact its own line with a reason, and name the criterion. Only then write the ratio. A correct answer with no reasons can lose more than half the marks, while a well-reasoned proof with a small slip at the end still earns most of them.

slides.heading: Quick check: perimeter of a similar triangle
slides.body_md: All sides scale by the same factor.
slides.narration: Find the scale factor by pairing the shortest sides. Then think: if every side is multiplied by the same number, what happens to the sum of the sides?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
bullets: AA: two pairs of equal angles. SSS: three side ratios equal. SAS: two side ratios equal and the included angles equal.
SSA is not a criterion.
Pair vertices by position in the similarity statement, then write the side ratios.
Shadows and lamp posts: right angles + a shared or equal angle $\Rightarrow$ AA.
Perimeters of similar triangles are in the same ratio as their sides.

rows: A line parallel to one side of a triangle
BPT for the two cut sides; AA for the ratio that includes the parallel side
Vertically opposite angles + one more angle or two side ratios
Right angles + equal sun or light angle ⇒ AA
SSS, after sorting each triangle’s sides from shortest to longest

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: a parallel line inside a triangle uses BPT and AA; crossing lines use vertically opposite angles; heights and shadows use right angles and equal light angles for AA; when only lengths are given, sort the sides and test SSS.

slides.narration: Let us recap part two. Three criteria, A A, S S S and S A S, prove triangles similar, but side side angle does not. Always match letters by position before writing ratios. For heights and shadows, look for the right angle and the shared or equal angle. The table shows the usual route for the situations you will meet most often.

slides.heading: Exam tips: criteria and applications
bullets: Similarity proof (3 or 5 marks): each equal angle or ratio with its reason earns a mark; naming the criterion earns a mark.
Wrong correspondence is the top error: from $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle QRP$, $AB$ pairs with $QR$, not $PQ$.
SAS: say why the angle is included. SSS: sort the sides first.
Word problems: draw and label the figure (1 mark), state the similar triangles with the criterion, then solve. Give units.
Lamp-post problems: the larger triangle uses post-to-tip distance, not just the shadow.
slides.narration: A few last tips. In a proof, every reason is worth marks, so write them all. Before writing any ratio, check the order of letters in your similarity statement. In word problems, a neat labelled figure usually earns the first mark, and the final answer needs its unit. And with lamp posts, remember that the big triangle reaches all the way from the post to the tip of the shadow.

notes.title: Triangles — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Similar figures
sections.body_md:
Two figures are **similar** when one is an exact enlargement or reduction of the other: they have the **same shape**, but not necessarily the same size. Two figures are **congruent** when they have the same shape **and** the same size.

Two polygons with the same number of sides are similar if and only if

1. all their corresponding angles are equal, **and**
2. all their corresponding sides are in the same ratio.

Both conditions matter. A square and a non-square rectangle have equal angles but are not similar; a square and a non-square rhombus have proportional sides but are not similar.

**Always similar:** any two circles, any two squares, any two equilateral triangles, any two line segments. **Not always similar:** rectangles, rhombuses, isosceles triangles, right triangles.

Every pair of congruent figures is similar (the ratio is 1), but similar figures need not be congruent.

*Not in the 2026–27 syllabus:* areas of similar triangles, and the proofs of Pythagoras' theorem and its converse.

key_terms.definition_md: Figures with the same shape; one is an enlargement or reduction of the other.
Figures with the same shape and size (symbol $\cong$).
The common ratio $k$ of corresponding sides. $k > 1$ enlarges, $k < 1$ reduces, $k = 1$ gives a congruent copy.
Angles or sides that occupy matching positions in two figures.

formulas.latex: \frac{\text{side of copy}}{\text{matching side of original}} = k \ \text{(the same for every pair)}
formulas.label: Scale factor

visual.alt: Left: square ABCD with side 2 cm. Middle: rectangle EFGH, 3.5 cm by 2 cm, with right angles like the square but sides not in one ratio. Right: rhombus IJKM with side 2 cm, sides in ratio 1 to 1 with the square but with a 60 degree angle instead of 90 degrees.
visual.caption: Square vs rectangle: angles equal, sides not proportional. Square vs rhombus: sides proportional, angles not equal. Neither pair is similar.

sections.heading: 2. Similar triangles and correspondence
sections.body_md:
$\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ is read "triangle $ABC$ is similar to triangle $PQR$". The **order of the letters** gives the correspondence: $A \leftrightarrow P$, $B \leftrightarrow Q$, $C \leftrightarrow R$. Therefore

- $\angle A = \angle P$, $\angle B = \angle Q$, $\angle C = \angle R$, and
- $\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{BC}{QR} = \dfrac{CA}{RP}$.

Side $AB$ joins the 1st and 2nd vertices, so it matches $PQ$, which joins the 1st and 2nd vertices of the other triangle. Never pair letters alphabetically: from $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle QRP$ you get $\dfrac{AB}{QR} = \dfrac{BC}{RP} = \dfrac{CA}{PQ}$.

Because every side is multiplied by the same $k$, the **perimeters** of similar triangles are also in the ratio $k$.

key_terms.definition_md: A statement such as $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ whose letter order fixes which vertices match.

formulas.latex: \triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR \iff \angle A = \angle P,\ \angle B = \angle Q,\ \angle C = \angle R \ \text{and} \ \frac{AB}{PQ} = \frac{BC}{QR} = \frac{CA}{RP}
formulas.label: Definition for triangles

rows: A ↔ Q, B ↔ R, C ↔ P

visual.alt: Table reading the statement triangle ABC similar to triangle QRP: A matches Q, B matches R, C matches P, so angle A equals angle Q and so on, and AB over QR equals BC over RP equals CA over PQ.
visual.caption: Read the letters position by position: 1st with 1st, 2nd with 2nd, 3rd with 3rd.

sections.heading: 3. Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales)
sections.body_md:
**Theorem.** If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.

In $\triangle ABC$ with $D$ on $AB$, $E$ on $AC$ and $DE \parallel BC$: $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$.

**Proof outline (learn it — it is examined).**
- *Construction:* join $BE$ and $CD$; draw $EM \perp AB$ and $DN \perp AC$.
- $\dfrac{\operatorname{ar}(ADE)}{\operatorname{ar}(BDE)} = \dfrac{AD}{DB}$, because both triangles have height $EM$ … (1)
- $\dfrac{\operatorname{ar}(ADE)}{\operatorname{ar}(DEC)} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$, because both triangles have height $DN$ … (2)
- $\operatorname{ar}(BDE) = \operatorname{ar}(DEC)$: same base $DE$, between the same parallels $DE$ and $BC$ … (3)
- From (1), (2), (3): $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$.

**Other forms** (add 1 to both sides and invert): $\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{AE}{AC}$ and $\dfrac{DB}{AB} = \dfrac{EC}{AC}$. Use the part-to-whole form when a whole side is given.

**Caution:** BPT is about the two **cut sides**. It does not give the length of $DE$. For that you need similarity: $\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{AD}{AB}$ (section 6).

**Consequence:** three (or more) parallel lines cut any two transversals in the same ratio. Prove it by joining a point on one transversal to a point on the other and applying BPT twice.

key_terms.definition_md: A line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio; also called Thales’ theorem.
A line that cuts two or more other lines.

visual.alt: The construction for the proof: in triangle ABC with DE parallel to BC, the segments BE and CD are joined, EM is drawn perpendicular to AB with M on AB, and DN is drawn perpendicular to AC with N on AC.
visual.caption: Construction: join BE and CD; draw EM ⊥ AB and DN ⊥ AC.

sections.heading: 4. Converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem
sections.body_md:
**Theorem (statement only).** If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, the line is parallel to the third side.

$\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC} \Longrightarrow DE \parallel BC$.

**How to use it.** To show two lines are parallel: (1) find both ratios separately, (2) show that they are equal, (3) conclude "$DE \parallel BC$ (converse of BPT)". If the ratios are unequal, the line is **not** parallel, because a parallel line would have to give equal ratios.

The proof of the converse is not required in the 2026–27 syllabus.

key_terms.definition_md: A statement with the "if" and "then" parts of a theorem swapped. It must be proved (or stated as a separate theorem); it is not automatically true.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with D on AB and E on AC. AD is 3 and DB is 4, AE is 3.3 and EC is 4.4, so both sides are cut in the ratio 3 to 4 and the dashed segment DE comes out parallel to BC.
visual.caption: Equal ratios (3 : 4 = 3.3 : 4.4) force DE ∥ BC.

sections.heading: 5. Criteria for similarity of triangles
sections.body_md:
For triangles, fewer facts are enough. State these criteria exactly; their proofs are not asked.

- **AAA / AA.** If the corresponding angles of two triangles are equal, the triangles are similar. Since the angles of a triangle add up to $180^\circ$, two pairs of equal angles are enough (AA).
- **SSS.** If the corresponding sides of two triangles are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar (and their corresponding angles are equal).
- **SAS.** If one angle of a triangle equals one angle of another and the sides **including** these angles are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar.

**SSA is not a criterion:** two sides and a non-included angle can fit two different triangles.

**Where equal angles hide in figures:** a common angle; vertically opposite angles; corresponding or alternate angles from parallel lines; right angles from perpendiculars, vertical poles or walls.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle formed between two given sides of a triangle.
Two pairs of equal corresponding angles prove two triangles similar.

The third pair is then equal automatically

A common or vertically opposite angle between the known sides
The equal angle must be the included angle

sections.heading: 6. Using similarity to find lengths
sections.body_md:
**Method.**
1. Name the two triangles and give the criterion with reasons ("$\angle A$ common; $\angle ADE = \angle ABC$, corresponding angles").
2. Write the similarity statement in the correct order.
3. Write all three side ratios from that order.
4. Use the pair of sides you know completely to find $k$, then find the unknown side. Check that all ratios agree.

**A parallel line inside a triangle.** If $DE \parallel BC$ in $\triangle ABC$, then $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$ (AA), so
$\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{DE}{BC}$. The parallel segment compares with the **whole** side.

**Crossing lines (X shape).** When $AC$ and $BD$ cross at $O$ and $AB \parallel CD$, $\triangle AOB \sim \triangle COD$ (alternate angles and vertically opposite angles). This is how trapezium diagonal problems are solved.

**"Crossed" similarity.** If $\dfrac{PS}{PR} = \dfrac{PT}{PQ}$ with a common angle $P$, then $\triangle PST \sim \triangle PRQ$ — $S$ matches $R$. Then $ST$ is usually **not** parallel to $QR$.

key_terms.definition_md: The ratio of a pair of sides known completely, used to find all other corresponding sides.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with median AD, so D is the midpoint of BC. A segment PQ parallel to BC meets AB at P, AD at R and AC at Q. Triangle APR is shaded inside the larger triangle ABD.
visual.caption: AD is a median (BD = DC) and PQ ∥ BC. Prove PR = RQ.

sections.heading: 7. Heights and distances with similar triangles
sections.body_md:
**Sun and shadows.** The sun's rays are parallel, so at one moment every vertical object on level ground forms a right triangle with its shadow, and all these triangles have the same angles (AA). Hence $\dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{shadow}}$ is the same for every object.

**Lamp posts.** Light spreads from a point. A person of height $h$ standing $d$ from a post of height $H$ has shadow $x$ with $\dfrac{h}{H} = \dfrac{x}{x + d}$, because both triangles share the angle at the shadow tip.

**Mirror method.** A mirror laid flat on level ground: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, so the eye triangle and the object triangle are similar: $\dfrac{\text{object height}}{\text{object–mirror distance}} = \dfrac{\text{eye height}}{\text{eye–mirror distance}}$.

**Sighting over a stick.** When the eye is above the ground, the similar triangles start at **eye level**: subtract the eye height from the vertical lengths first.

Conditions to state: same moment (for shadows), level ground, objects vertical.

key_terms.term: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection
key_terms.definition_md: A ray reflected from a flat mirror makes equal angles with the mirror on both sides, which gives the equal angles needed for AA.

sections.heading: 8. Writing proofs for full marks
sections.body_md:
Board marking schemes award marks for each justified step, so a proof is graded line by line.

1. **Figure** — draw and label it, including any construction (usually 1 mark).
2. **Given / To prove / Construction** — one line each.
3. **Statements with reasons** — one fact per line; the reason in brackets: (common), (vertically opposite angles), (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$), (BPT), (converse of BPT).
4. **Criterion** — "$\therefore \triangle APR \sim \triangle ABD$ (AA)", with the vertices in matching order.
5. **Conclusion** — finish with exactly what was asked, then "Hence proved."

A correct final line with no reasons earns little; a well-reasoned proof with a small slip at the end still earns most of the marks.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *State and prove BPT* (5 marks): statement with given and to prove 1, figure with construction 1, each area ratio 1 + 1, equal areas with the reason "same base, between the same parallels" and the conclusion 1.
- *Similarity proofs* (3–5 marks): each equal angle or ratio **with its reason** earns marks; naming the criterion earns a mark; the final ratio or result earns a mark.
- *Word problems* (shadows, lamp posts, mirrors, rivers): a labelled figure 1, similar triangles with criterion 1, correct proportion 1, answer with unit 1.

**Common mistakes**
1. Wrong correspondence: pairing letters alphabetically instead of by position in the similarity statement.
2. Writing $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{DE}{BC}$. The parallel segment compares with the whole side: $\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{AD}{AB}$.
3. Using SAS with an angle that is not between the two proportional sides (that is SSA).
4. In SSS, pairing sides in the order given instead of shortest-with-shortest.
5. Lamp-post problems: using the distance $d$ instead of $x + d$ for the big triangle.
6. Sighting problems: forgetting to subtract eye height.
7. Saying "by BPT" when proving lines parallel; the reason is "converse of BPT".
8. Leaving out units, or mixing metres and centimetres.

cards.front_md: What are **similar figures**?
cards.back_md: Figures with the same shape but not necessarily the same size; one is an enlargement or reduction of the other.

cards.front_md: What are **congruent figures**?
cards.back_md: Figures with the same shape **and** the same size ($\cong$).

cards.front_md: Two conditions for two polygons to be similar?
cards.back_md: (1) All corresponding angles equal **and** (2) all corresponding sides in the same ratio.

cards.front_md: Name a pair of quadrilaterals with equal angles that are **not** similar.
cards.back_md: A square and a non-square rectangle: all angles 90°, but the side ratios differ.

cards.front_md: Name a pair of quadrilaterals with proportional sides that are **not** similar.
cards.back_md: A square and a non-square rhombus: side ratio 1 : 1 everywhere, but the angles differ.

cards.front_md: Which figures are **always** similar?
cards.back_md: Any two circles, squares, equilateral triangles or line segments.

cards.front_md: Are congruent figures similar?
cards.back_md: Yes, with scale factor 1. Similar figures need not be congruent.

cards.front_md: What is the **scale factor**?
cards.back_md: The common ratio $k$ of corresponding sides of similar figures.

cards.front_md: From $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle QRP$, which side matches $AB$?
cards.back_md: $QR$ — pair letters by position: $A \leftrightarrow Q$, $B \leftrightarrow R$, $C \leftrightarrow P$.

cards.front_md: Ratios from $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{BC}{QR} = \dfrac{CA}{RP}$

cards.front_md: State the **Basic Proportionality Theorem**.
cards.back_md: If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to meet the other two sides at distinct points, it divides those sides in the same ratio.

cards.front_md: BPT in symbols ($DE \parallel BC$ in $\triangle ABC$)?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$

cards.front_md: Part-to-whole forms of BPT?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{AE}{AC}$ and $\dfrac{DB}{AB} = \dfrac{EC}{AC}$

cards.front_md: Another name for BPT?
cards.back_md: Thales’ theorem.

cards.front_md: BPT proof: what is the construction?
cards.back_md: Join $BE$ and $CD$; draw $EM \perp AB$ and $DN \perp AC$.

cards.front_md: BPT proof: where is the parallel line used?
cards.back_md: To show $\operatorname{ar}(BDE) = \operatorname{ar}(DEC)$: same base $DE$, between the same parallels $DE$ and $BC$.

cards.front_md: State the **converse of BPT**.
cards.back_md: If a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, it is parallel to the third side.

cards.front_md: Proving two lines parallel from lengths: what reason do you write?
cards.back_md: "Converse of BPT" — after showing both ratios separately are equal.

cards.front_md: Three parallel lines cut two transversals. What is true?
cards.back_md: The intercepts on the two transversals are in the same ratio.

cards.front_md: State the **AA criterion**.
cards.back_md: If two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, the triangles are similar.

cards.front_md: Why are two pairs of angles enough?
cards.back_md: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°, so the third pair is automatically equal.

cards.front_md: State the **SSS criterion**.
cards.back_md: If the three sides of one triangle are in the same ratio to the three sides of another, the triangles are similar.

cards.front_md: State the **SAS criterion**.
cards.back_md: If one angle of a triangle equals one angle of another and the sides including these angles are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar.

cards.front_md: Is SSA a similarity criterion?
cards.back_md: No. Two sides with a non-included angle can fit two different triangles.

cards.front_md: Where do equal angles usually come from in a figure?
cards.back_md: Common angle, vertically opposite angles, corresponding/alternate angles from parallels, right angles.

cards.front_md: $DE \parallel BC$ in $\triangle ABC$: what is $\dfrac{DE}{BC}$?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{AD}{AB}$ (similar triangles) — not $\dfrac{AD}{DB}$.

cards.front_md: Using SSS: how do you pair the sides?
cards.back_md: Sort each triangle’s sides from shortest to longest and pair them in that order.

cards.front_md: Perimeters of similar triangles?
cards.back_md: In the same ratio as their corresponding sides.

cards.front_md: Why do shadows give similar triangles?
cards.back_md: Objects are vertical (right angles) and the sun’s rays are parallel (equal angles with level ground) ⇒ AA.

cards.front_md: Lamp post height H, person height h at distance d: shadow x?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{h}{H} = \dfrac{x}{x + d}$

cards.front_md: Mirror method: why are the triangles similar?
cards.back_md: Right angles at the person and the object; equal angles at the mirror (incidence = reflection) ⇒ AA.

cards.front_md: Sighting a treetop over a stick: what must you subtract?
cards.back_md: The eye height — the similar triangles start at eye level, not at the ground.

cards.back_md: $\triangle AOB \sim \triangle COD$ (SAS, vertically opposite angles), so $AB \parallel CD$ (alternate angles).

cards.back_md: Wrong correspondence of vertices. Always write the similarity statement in matching order before writing ratios.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of figures is **always** similar?
questions.solution_md:
Every equilateral triangle has all angles $60^\circ$, and its three sides are equal, so for any two equilateral triangles every side ratio is the same. Both conditions hold, so they are always similar.

The others can fail: rectangles $4 \times 2$ and $4 \times 3$ have equal angles but unequal side ratios; a square and a tilted rhombus have equal side ratios but unequal angles; isosceles triangles with apex angles $40^\circ$ and $100^\circ$ have different angles.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c): equal angles (60° each) and constant side ratio

questions.stem_md: A photograph measures 15 cm by 10 cm. It is enlarged so that the shorter side becomes 25 cm. For the enlargement to be similar to the original, the longer side must be
questions.solution_md: Scale factor $k = \dfrac{25}{10} = 2.5$. Longer side $= 15 \times 2.5 = 37.5$ cm. (Adding 15 cm to both sides gives 30 cm, which changes the shape — a common wrong idea.)

marking_scheme.step: Scale factor 2.5 applied to 15 cm: option (c)

questions.stem_md: If $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle QRP$, which of the following is true?
questions.solution_md: Pair the vertices by position: $A \leftrightarrow Q$, $B \leftrightarrow R$, $C \leftrightarrow P$. So $AB \leftrightarrow QR$, $BC \leftrightarrow RP$, $CA \leftrightarrow PQ$, giving $\dfrac{AB}{QR} = \dfrac{BC}{RP} = \dfrac{CA}{PQ}$. Option (d) pairs the letters alphabetically, which is the classic error.

marking_scheme.step: Correct correspondence A–Q, B–R, C–P: option (a)

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ and $E$ are points on $AB$ and $AC$ such that $DE \parallel BC$. Which of the following is **not** necessarily true?
questions.solution_md: (a) is the Basic Proportionality Theorem; (b) and (d) follow from it (add 1 to both sides and invert). The parallel segment compares with the **whole** side: $\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{AD}{AB}$, not $\dfrac{AD}{DB}$. For example, if $AD = 2$, $DB = 3$ and $BC = 10$, then $DE = 4$, but $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac23 \neq \dfrac{4}{10}$.

marking_scheme.step: Identifies (c): DE/BC equals AD/AB, not AD/DB

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle PQR$, a line $ST \parallel QR$ meets $PQ$ at $S$ and $PR$ at $T$. If $PS = 2$ cm, $SQ = 5$ cm and $PT = 3$ cm, then $TR$ is
questions.solution_md: By BPT, $\dfrac{PS}{SQ} = \dfrac{PT}{TR}$, so $\dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{3}{TR}$ and $TR = \dfrac{5 \times 3}{2} = 7.5$ cm.

marking_scheme.step: BPT ratio set up and solved: option (b)

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$ with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$. If $AD = x + 1$, $DB = 3x - 1$, $AE = x + 3$ and $EC = 3x + 4$ (all in cm), then $x$ equals

marking_scheme.step: Forms the BPT equation and solves x = 7: option (c)

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is **not** a criterion for the similarity of two triangles?
questions.solution_md: AA, SSS and SAS are the similarity criteria. Two sides and a **non-included** angle (SSA) can fit two differently shaped triangles, so it does not prove similarity.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$, $\dfrac{AB}{DE} = \dfrac{AC}{DF}$ and $\angle A = \angle D$. Then

options.text_md: the triangles need not be similar

questions.solution_md: $\angle A$ lies between sides $AB$ and $AC$, and $\angle D$ lies between $DE$ and $DF$, so the equal angles are the **included** angles of the proportional sides. By SAS, $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ with $A \leftrightarrow D$, $B \leftrightarrow E$, $C \leftrightarrow F$. SSS is wrong because only two ratios are known.

marking_scheme.step: Included angle recognised, SAS with correct order: option (a)

questions.stem_md: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ with $AB = 4$ cm, $PQ = 10$ cm and $QR = 12.5$ cm. Then $BC$ is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{BC}{QR} = \dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{4}{10}$, so $BC = 0.4 \times 12.5 = 5$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A vertical stick 1.2 m long casts a shadow 0.9 m long on level ground. At the same time, a mobile tower casts a shadow 27 m long. The height of the tower is
questions.solution_md: Same time, level ground: the triangles are similar (AA), so $\dfrac{h}{27} = \dfrac{1.2}{0.9}$ and $h = \dfrac{1.2 \times 27}{0.9} = 36$ m. Option (a) comes from inverting the ratio.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A = 50^\circ$ and $\angle B = 60^\circ$. In $\triangle PQR$, $\angle P = 70^\circ$ and $\angle Q = 50^\circ$. Which statement is correct?
questions.solution_md:
$\angle C = 180^\circ - 50^\circ - 60^\circ = 70^\circ$ and $\angle R = 180^\circ - 70^\circ - 50^\circ = 60^\circ$.

Match equal angles: $A\,(50^\circ) \leftrightarrow Q$, $B\,(60^\circ) \leftrightarrow R$, $C\,(70^\circ) \leftrightarrow P$. So $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle QRP$ (AA).

marking_scheme.step: Third angles found and vertices matched: option (b)

questions.stem_md: The sides of a triangle are 6 cm, 8 cm and 9 cm. The shortest side of a similar triangle is 9 cm. The perimeter of the second triangle is
questions.solution_md: Scale factor $k = \dfrac{9}{6} = 1.5$. Perimeter of the first triangle $= 6 + 8 + 9 = 23$ cm, so the second is $23 \times 1.5 = 34.5$ cm (sides $9$, $12$, $13.5$ cm).

marking_scheme.step: Scale factor 1.5 applied to perimeter 23 cm: option (b)

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle XYZ$, $M$ and $N$ lie on $XY$ and $XZ$ with $MN \parallel YZ$. If $XM : MY = 2 : 3$ and $XZ = 12.5$ cm, then $XN$ is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{XN}{XZ} = \dfrac{XM}{XY} = \dfrac{2}{2+3} = \dfrac25$, so $XN = \dfrac25 \times 12.5 = 5$ cm. Option (d) wrongly uses $\dfrac{XN}{XZ} = \dfrac23$.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ is a point on $BC$ such that $\angle BAD = \angle BCA$. If $AB = 6$ cm and $BD = 4$ cm, then $BC$ is
questions.solution_md:
In $\triangle BAD$ and $\triangle BCA$: $\angle B$ is common and $\angle BAD = \angle BCA$, so $\triangle BAD \sim \triangle BCA$ (AA).

Hence $\dfrac{BA}{BC} = \dfrac{BD}{BA}$, so $BC = \dfrac{BA^2}{BD} = \dfrac{36}{4} = 9$ cm.

marking_scheme.step: AA similarity with correct correspondence, BC = 9 cm: option (b)

questions.stem_md: Two polygons with the same number of sides are similar if

options.text_md: their corresponding angles are equal and their corresponding sides are proportional

questions.solution_md: Both conditions are needed for polygons in general: a square and a non-square rectangle have equal angles but are not similar; a square and a non-square rhombus have proportional sides but are not similar.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ is a point on $AB$ and $E$ is a point on $AC$ with $AD = 3.6$ cm, $AB = 9$ cm and $AE = 2.4$ cm. For $DE$ to be parallel to $BC$, the length of $AC$ must be
questions.solution_md: By the converse of BPT, $DE \parallel BC$ when $\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{AE}{AC}$, i.e. $\dfrac{3.6}{9} = \dfrac{2.4}{AC}$, so $AC = \dfrac{2.4 \times 9}{3.6} = 6$ cm.

marking_scheme.step: Equal part-to-whole ratios give AC = 6 cm: option (b)

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$ with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$. If $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac23$, then $\dfrac{DE}{BC}$ equals
questions.solution_md: $DE \parallel BC$ gives $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$ (AA: common $\angle A$, corresponding angles). So $\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{2}{2+3} = \dfrac25$. Option (a) compares with the part $DB$ instead of the whole side $AB$.

questions.stem_md: $ABCD$ is a trapezium with $AB \parallel DC$ and $AB = 2\,DC$. Its diagonals meet at $O$. If $OC = 3.5$ cm, then $AC$ is
questions.solution_md:
In $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle COD$: $\angle OAB = \angle OCD$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$) and $\angle AOB = \angle COD$ (vertically opposite). So $\triangle AOB \sim \triangle COD$ (AA) and $\dfrac{AO}{OC} = \dfrac{AB}{CD} = 2$.

$AO = 7$ cm, so $AC = AO + OC = 10.5$ cm. Option (a) stops at $AO$.

marking_scheme.step: AA similarity, AO = 7 cm, AC = 10.5 cm: option (b)

questions.stem_md: A family photo measuring 12 cm by 8 cm is mounted with a 1 cm wide border all round, making a 14 cm by 10 cm rectangle. Are the photo and the outer rectangle similar?

options.text_md: Yes, because all their angles are 90°
Yes, because the border has the same width everywhere
No, because two rectangles can never be similar

questions.solution_md: The angles are all $90^\circ$, but the side ratios differ: $\dfrac{12}{14} \approx 0.857$ while $\dfrac{8}{10} = 0.8$. Adding the same amount to each side does not keep the shape, so they are not similar. Option (d) is false: a $6 \times 4$ and a $9 \times 6$ rectangle are similar.

marking_scheme.step: Compares the two side ratios: option (c)

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 9$ cm and $AC = 12$ cm. Points $P$ on $AB$ and $Q$ on $AC$ are such that $\triangle APQ \sim \triangle ACB$ and $AP = 4$ cm. Then $AQ$ is
questions.solution_md:
From $\triangle APQ \sim \triangle ACB$: $A \leftrightarrow A$, $P \leftrightarrow C$, $Q \leftrightarrow B$. So $\dfrac{AP}{AC} = \dfrac{AQ}{AB}$, giving $\dfrac{4}{12} = \dfrac{AQ}{9}$ and $AQ = 3$ cm.

Option (b) comes from the wrong pairing $\dfrac{AP}{AB} = \dfrac{AQ}{AC}$, which would be true only if $PQ \parallel BC$.

marking_scheme.step: Reads the correspondence P–C, Q–B and finds AQ = 3 cm: option (a)

**Assertion (A):** Any two congruent triangles are also similar.

**Assertion (A):** In $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$ with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$. If $AD = 2$ cm, $DB = 3$ cm and $AE = 4$ cm, then $EC = 6$ cm.

**Assertion (A):** If $\angle A = \angle D$ and $\angle B = \angle E$ in $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$, then $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$.

**Reason (R):** If two triangles are similar, their corresponding sides are equal.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** $\triangle ABC$ with $AB = 3$ cm, $BC = 4$ cm, $\angle B = 40^\circ$ and $\triangle PQR$ with $PQ = 6$ cm, $QR = 8$ cm, $\angle R = 40^\circ$ are similar.

**Reason (R):** For the SAS similarity criterion, the equal angles must be included between the pairs of proportional sides.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: In $\triangle ABC$ the $40^\circ$ angle is at $B$, between $AB$ and $BC$. In $\triangle PQR$ the $40^\circ$ angle is at $R$, which is **not** between $PQ$ and $QR$ (their included angle is $\angle Q$). SAS cannot be used. In fact the triangles are not similar: $\triangle ABC$ has angles of about $40^\circ$, $91.4^\circ$ and $48.6^\circ$, while in $\triangle PQR$, $\sin P = \dfrac{8 \sin 40^\circ}{6}$ gives $\angle P \approx 59^\circ$ or $121^\circ$, so its angles are about $40^\circ, 59^\circ, 81^\circ$ or $40^\circ, 121^\circ, 19^\circ$ — neither matches. (This check uses trigonometry and is beyond the question; the SAS reasoning is what is expected.) A is false, R is true: (d).

questions.stem_md: Every pair of congruent figures is also a pair of similar figures.
questions.solution_md: Congruent figures have equal corresponding angles and their corresponding sides are in the ratio 1 : 1, so both conditions for similarity hold. True.

questions.stem_md: Any two right-angled triangles are similar.
questions.solution_md: Only one pair of angles (the right angles) is guaranteed equal. A right triangle with angles $90^\circ, 30^\circ, 60^\circ$ is not similar to one with $90^\circ, 45^\circ, 45^\circ$. False.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, if $DE \parallel BC$ with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$, then $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{DE}{BC}$.
questions.solution_md: The correct relation is $\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{AD}{AB}$ (from $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$). With $AD = 1$, $DB = 1$ and $BC = 6$: $DE = 3$, so $\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac12$ but $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = 1$. False.

questions.stem_md: If the three angles of one triangle are equal to the three angles of another triangle, the two triangles are similar.
questions.solution_md: This is the AAA (equivalently AA) similarity criterion. True.

questions.stem_md: A triangle with sides 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm is similar to a triangle with sides 4 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm.
questions.solution_md: Pair the sides in order of size: $\dfrac42 = 2$, $\dfrac63 = 2$, but $\dfrac74 = 1.75$. The three ratios are not all equal, so SSS fails. False.

questions.stem_md: All ___ triangles are similar to each other.
questions.solution_md: Equilateral triangles always have angles $60^\circ, 60^\circ, 60^\circ$ and equal sides, so any two are similar.

questions.stem_md: The Basic Proportionality Theorem is also known as ___ theorem.
questions.solution_md: It is named after the Greek mathematician Thales of Miletus.

questions.stem_md: If $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ with $AB = 5$ cm and $DE = 7.5$ cm, then every side of $\triangle DEF$ is ___ times the corresponding side of $\triangle ABC$.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{DE}{AB} = \dfrac{7.5}{5} = 1.5$, and the same ratio holds for every pair of corresponding sides.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle PQR$, $XY \parallel QR$ with $X$ on $PQ$ and $Y$ on $PR$. If $\dfrac{PX}{XQ} = \dfrac34$, then $\dfrac{PY}{PR} =$ ___ .
questions.solution_md: By BPT, $\dfrac{PY}{YR} = \dfrac{PX}{XQ} = \dfrac34$. So $PY : PR = 3 : (3 + 4) = 3 : 7$, i.e. $\dfrac37$.

questions.stem_md: A 2 m tall pole casts a 3 m shadow. At the same time, a building casts a 45 m shadow on the same level ground. The height of the building is ___ m.
questions.solution_md: Similar triangles (AA): $\dfrac{h}{45} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, so $h = 30$ m.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$ with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$. $AD = 3.2$ cm, $DB = 4.8$ cm and $AC = 9$ cm. Find $AE$ in cm.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $AB = 3.2 + 4.8 = 8$ cm.

**Step 2.** By BPT, $\dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{3.2}{8} = 0.4$.

**Step 3.** $AE = 0.4 \times 9 = 3.6$ cm.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle LMN$, $PQ \parallel MN$ with $P$ on $LM$ and $Q$ on $LN$. If $LP = 2.5$ cm, $PM = 3.5$ cm and $QN = 4.9$ cm, find $LQ$ in cm.
questions.solution_md:
By BPT, $\dfrac{LP}{PM} = \dfrac{LQ}{QN}$, so $\dfrac{2.5}{3.5} = \dfrac{LQ}{4.9}$.

$LQ = \dfrac{2.5 \times 4.9}{3.5} = 3.5$ cm.

questions.stem_md: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$. $AB = 3.6$ cm, $BC = 4.8$ cm, $CA = 6$ cm and $DE = 5.4$ cm. Find the perimeter of $\triangle DEF$ in cm.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** Scale factor $k = \dfrac{DE}{AB} = \dfrac{5.4}{3.6} = 1.5$.

**Step 2.** Perimeter of $\triangle ABC = 3.6 + 4.8 + 6 = 14.4$ cm.

**Step 3.** Every side is multiplied by $1.5$, so the perimeter of $\triangle DEF = 1.5 \times 14.4 = 21.6$ cm ($EF = 7.2$, $FD = 9$).

questions.stem_md: A street lamp in Jaipur is fixed 7.2 m above the ground. A boy 1.2 m tall stands 4 m from the foot of the lamp post. Find the length of his shadow in metres.
questions.solution_md:
Let the shadow be $x$ m. The boy and the post are vertical, and the light ray through the top of his head reaches the shadow tip, so the small and large triangles share the angle at the tip (AA).

$\dfrac{1.2}{7.2} = \dfrac{x}{x + 4}$, so $7.2x = 1.2x + 4.8$, giving $6x = 4.8$ and $x = 0.8$ m.

marking_scheme.step: Similar triangles with base x + 4 for the post

questions.stem_md: India Gate in New Delhi is 42 m tall. At a moment when a girl 1.5 m tall casts a shadow 2.1 m long, how long is the shadow of India Gate on the level ground around it? Give the answer in metres.
questions.solution_md:
At the same moment the sun's rays are parallel, so the girl's triangle and the monument's triangle are similar (AA).

$\dfrac{s}{42} = \dfrac{2.1}{1.5}$, so $s = \dfrac{42 \times 2.1}{1.5} = 58.8$ m.

questions.stem_md: To find the height of the school flagpole in Bhopal, Ananya lays a small mirror flat on the level ground 6 m from the foot of the pole. She stands 1.2 m from the mirror, on the other side, and just sees the top of the pole in the mirror. Her eyes are 1.44 m above the ground. Find the height of the flagpole in metres.
questions.solution_md:
Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, so the rays to the eye and from the pole-top make equal angles with the ground at the mirror. Both the girl and the pole are vertical, so the two right triangles are similar (AA).

$\dfrac{h}{6} = \dfrac{1.44}{1.2}$, so $h = \dfrac{1.44 \times 6}{1.2} = 7.2$ m.

marking_scheme.step: Recognises similar right triangles at the mirror (AA)

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle PQR$, $ST \parallel QR$ with $S$ on $PQ$ and $T$ on $PR$. If $PS : SQ = 3 : 5$ and $QR = 12$ cm, find $ST$ in cm.
questions.solution_md:
$ST \parallel QR$ gives $\triangle PST \sim \triangle PQR$ (AA: common $\angle P$, corresponding angles $\angle PST = \angle PQR$).

So $\dfrac{ST}{QR} = \dfrac{PS}{PQ} = \dfrac{3}{3+5} = \dfrac38$, and $ST = \dfrac38 \times 12 = 4.5$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A wheelchair ramp at a school in Chennai rises 0.6 m over a horizontal distance of 2.4 m. A vertical support post is fixed under the ramp at a horizontal distance of 1.6 m from the lower end. Find the height of the post in metres.
questions.solution_md:
The post and the end of the ramp are both vertical, and the two triangles share the angle at the lower end, so they are similar (AA).

$\dfrac{h}{0.6} = \dfrac{1.6}{2.4}$, so $h = 0.6 \times \dfrac23 = 0.4$ m.

marking_scheme.step: Similar triangles sharing the angle at the lower end

questions.stem_md: At a Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata, two vertical bamboo poles 6 m and 9 m tall stand 15 m apart on level ground. A string runs from the top of each pole to the foot of the other. How high above the ground do the two strings cross? Give the answer in metres.
questions.solution_md:
Let the poles be $AB = 6$ m and $CD = 9$ m with feet $B$, $D$, and let the strings $AD$ and $CB$ cross at $O$, at height $h$ above the point $M$ on the ground. Let $BM = x$, so $MD = 15 - x$.

**Step 1.** $OM \parallel AB$: in $\triangle DAB$, $\triangle DOM \sim \triangle DAB$ (AA), so $\dfrac{h}{6} = \dfrac{15 - x}{15}$.

**Step 2.** $OM \parallel CD$: in $\triangle BCD$, $\triangle BOM \sim \triangle BCD$ (AA), so $\dfrac{h}{9} = \dfrac{x}{15}$.

**Step 3.** Add: $\dfrac{h}{6} + \dfrac{h}{9} = \dfrac{15 - x + x}{15} = 1$, so $h \cdot \dfrac{5}{18} = 1$ and $h = 3.6$ m.

(The answer does not depend on the 15 m gap: $h = \dfrac{6 \times 9}{6 + 9}$.)

marking_scheme.step: Two pairs of similar triangles with the crossing height
Eliminates x and gets h = 3.6 m

questions.stem_md: A model of a triangular roof truss is similar to the real truss, with every length in the model one-fortieth of the real length. The base of the model is 22.5 cm. Find the base of the real truss in metres.
questions.solution_md: Real base $= 40 \times 22.5 = 900$ cm $= 9$ m.

questions.stem_md: Give (i) one example of two figures that are similar but not congruent, and (ii) one example of two quadrilaterals whose corresponding angles are equal but which are not similar. Justify each in one line.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A circle of radius 2 cm and a circle of radius 5 cm (or a 1 cm square and a 3 cm square): same shape, different size.

(ii) A square of side 4 cm and a rectangle 4 cm by 6 cm: all angles are $90^\circ$, but $\dfrac44 \neq \dfrac46$, so the sides are not proportional.

questions.solution_md: Similar figures need the same shape; congruent figures also need the same size, so any enlargement works for (i). For (ii), equal angles alone do not fix the shape of a quadrilateral, so a square and a non-square rectangle work.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) valid example with the unequal side ratios shown

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$ with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$. If $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac45$ and $AC = 18$ cm, find $AE$ and $EC$.

answer.model_answer_md: By BPT, $\dfrac{AE}{EC} = \dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac45$. So $AE = \dfrac{4}{9} \times 18 = 8$ cm and $EC = 18 - 8 = 10$ cm.

**Step 1.** BPT: $AE : EC = 4 : 5$.

**Step 2.** Split $AC = 18$ cm in the ratio $4 : 5$: $AE = \dfrac{4}{9} \times 18 = 8$ cm, $EC = \dfrac59 \times 18 = 10$ cm.

**Check:** $\dfrac{8}{10} = \dfrac45$. ✓

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle PQR$, $S$ and $T$ are points on $PQ$ and $PR$ such that $PS = 1.5$ cm, $PQ = 4.5$ cm, $PT = 2$ cm and $PR = 6$ cm. Is $ST \parallel QR$? Justify your answer.

answer.model_answer_md: $SQ = 4.5 - 1.5 = 3$ cm and $TR = 6 - 2 = 4$ cm. $\dfrac{PS}{SQ} = \dfrac{1.5}{3} = \dfrac12$ and $\dfrac{PT}{TR} = \dfrac24 = \dfrac12$. The ratios are equal, so by the converse of BPT, $ST \parallel QR$. Yes.

questions.solution_md: Find the remaining parts, compare the two ratios, and conclude using the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem.

marking_scheme.step: Conclusion ST ∥ QR citing the converse of BPT

questions.stem_md: Check whether a triangle with sides 4 cm, 6 cm and 8 cm and a triangle with sides 6 cm, 9 cm and 12 cm are similar. If they are, name the criterion and give the scale factor of the larger triangle to the smaller.

answer.model_answer_md: Pairing sides in order of size: $\dfrac64 = \dfrac96 = \dfrac{12}{8} = 1.5$. All three ratios are equal, so the triangles are similar by the **SSS** criterion, with scale factor $1.5$.

questions.solution_md: Sort both sets of sides from shortest to longest, divide matching sides, and compare all three ratios.

questions.stem_md:
Say whether each pair of triangles must be similar. Give a reason.

(i) One triangle has angles 40° and 60°; the other has angles 60° and 80°.

(ii) One triangle has two sides 5 cm and 6 cm with a 50° angle between them; the other has sides 10 cm and 12 cm and a 50° angle opposite the 12 cm side.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Third angles: $180^\circ - 40^\circ - 60^\circ = 80^\circ$ and $180^\circ - 60^\circ - 80^\circ = 40^\circ$. Both triangles have angles $40^\circ, 60^\circ, 80^\circ$, so they are similar (AA).

(ii) Not necessarily. The ratios $\dfrac{10}{5} = \dfrac{12}{6}$ are equal, but in the second triangle the $50^\circ$ angle is **not** between the 10 cm and 12 cm sides, so SAS does not apply.

$AB \leftrightarrow FD$ and $BC \leftrightarrow EF$ share $B \leftrightarrow F$; $AB \leftrightarrow FD$ and $CA \leftrightarrow DE$ share $A \leftrightarrow D$; so $C \leftrightarrow E$. Hence $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DFE$.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$ with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$. If $AD = 2x$, $DB = 3x + 1$, $AE = 2x + 2$ and $EC = 3x + 5$ (in cm), find $x$ and the lengths $AD$ and $AE$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$XY = 10$ cm. By BPT, $\dfrac{XM}{XZ} = \dfrac{XL}{XY} = \dfrac{4}{10}$, so $XM = 5$ cm and $MZ = 7.5$ cm.

$LM \parallel YZ$ gives $\triangle XLM \sim \triangle XYZ$ (AA), so $\dfrac{LM}{YZ} = \dfrac{XL}{XY}$ and $YZ = \dfrac{3.6 \times 10}{4} = 9$ cm.

questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $XY = 4 + 6 = 10$ cm.

**Step 2.** BPT (part-to-whole): $XM = \dfrac{4}{10} \times 12.5 = 5$ cm; $MZ = 12.5 - 5 = 7.5$ cm.

**Step 3.** $\angle X$ common and $\angle XLM = \angle XYZ$ (corresponding angles), so $\triangle XLM \sim \triangle XYZ$ (AA). Then $\dfrac{LM}{YZ} = \dfrac{XL}{XY}$ gives $YZ = 9$ cm. Note that $YZ$ needs similarity: BPT alone says nothing about $LM$.
